q: Who is the playwright of the one-act play "The Proposal"?
o: Anton Chekhov
Leo Tolstoy
Maxim Gorky
Ruskin Bond
e: Russian dramatist and short-story writer Anton Chekhov wrote the famous one-act farce "The Proposal" (1888-89).

q: What literary form is "The Proposal" in the Class 10 First Flight textbook?
o: A travelogue
A historical biography
A lyric poem
A one-act play (farce)
e: "The Proposal" is a humorous one-act play (farce) set in a Russian country house drawing room.

q: What is the full name of Lomov in the play?
o: Mikhail Petrovitch Lomov
Stepan Stepanovitch Lomov
Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov
Vassily Ivanovitch Lomov
e: The character list introduces Lomov as Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov, Chubukov's neighbour.

q: How old is Lomov when he comes to propose to Natalya?
o: Twenty-five years
Thirty-five years
Thirty years
Forty-five years
e: Lomov states in his monologue that he is already thirty-five, which he calls "a critical age".

q: What is the full name of Chubukov's daughter?
o: Elena Vassilevna
Natalya Stepanovna
Olga Ivanovna
Nastasya Mihailovna
e: Chubukov's daughter is Natalya Stepanovna (Stepanovna meaning daughter of Stepan).

q: How old is Natalya Stepanovna according to Lomov?
o: Twenty-five years old
Thirty years old
Eighteen years old
Twenty-one years old
e: While justifying his decision to marry her, Lomov mentions, "She's twenty-five years old."

q: What is the full name of Natalya's father?
o: Ivan Stepanovitch Chubukov
Mironov Stepanovitch Chubukov
Pyotr Vassilevitch Chubukov
Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov
e: The landowner father of Natalya is Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov.

q: What is the social relationship between Chubukov and Lomov?
o: Lawyer and client
Doctor and patient
Neighbouring landowners
Master and servant
e: Lomov is a neighbouring landowner whose estate borders Chubukov's estate.

q: What clothes is Lomov wearing when he arrives at Chubukov's house?
o: Casual farm clothes
A hunting coat and boots
An evening dress-jacket and white gloves
A soldier's uniform
e: The stage direction states that Lomov enters wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves (evening dress).

q: What is the real purpose of Lomov's visit to Chubukov's house?
o: To sell his horse
To ask for Natalya's hand in marriage
To borrow three hundred roubles
To invite them to a ball
e: Lomov comes formally dressed to ask Chubukov for his daughter Natalya's hand in marriage.

q: What does Chubukov initially think Lomov has come for when he hesitates?
o: To borrow money
To complain about his dog
To invite him for dinner
To buy Oxen Meadows
e: In an aside, Chubukov mutters, "He's come to borrow money. Shan't give him any!"

q: What household chore is Natalya doing when she enters the room to meet Lomov?
o: Polishing silverware
Knitting a sweater
Baking bread
Shelling peas for drying
e: Natalya enters wearing an apron and remarks that she has been shelling peas for drying.

q: What is the name of the piece of land over which Lomov and Natalya first quarrel?
o: Burnt Marsh
Birchwoods
Marusinsky Field
Oxen Meadows
e: The first bitter argument erupts when Lomov refers to "my Oxen Meadows," which Natalya claims belong to her family.

q: How large is Oxen Meadows according to Lomov?
o: Fifty dessiatins
One hundred acres
Nearly five dessiatins
Nearly two dessiatins
e: Lomov states that Oxen Meadows are "nearly five dessiatins, and are worth perhaps 300 roubles."

q: What is the approximate monetary value of Oxen Meadows mentioned by Lomov?
o: 1000 roubles
300 roubles
85 roubles
125 roubles
e: Lomov estimates the value of Oxen Meadows at around 300 roubles, saying it is the principle that matters to him.

q: Between which two landmarks does Lomov say Oxen Meadows are wedged?
o: Chubukov's birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh
The river and the railway station
Mironov's farm and the church
The village well and the forest
e: Lomov explains that his Oxen Meadows are wedged in between Chubukov's birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh.

q: According to Lomov, what were Chubukov's peasants supposed to do in return for using Oxen Meadows?
o: Make bricks for Lomov's aunt's grandmother
Harvest wheat for Lomov
Guard the birchwoods
Pay rent in gold coins
e: Lomov claims his aunt's grandmother gave free use of the Meadows to the peasants in return for making bricks for her.

q: For how many years did the peasants have free use of Oxen Meadows according to Lomov?
o: Three hundred years
Ten years
One hundred years
Forty years
e: Lomov says the peasants had free use of the Meadows for forty years and got into the habit of thinking them their own.

q: For how long do Natalya and Chubukov claim Oxen Meadows have belonged to their family?
o: Nearly forty years
Nearly one hundred years
Nearly three hundred years
About twenty-five years
e: Natalya insists, "We've had the land for nearly three hundred years, and then we're suddenly told that it isn't ours!"

q: What frequent physical complaint does Lomov suffer from whenever he gets excited?
o: Loss of hearing
Heart palpitations and a twitching eyebrow
Severe toothache
High fever and cough
e: Throughout the play, Lomov repeatedly complains of palpitations, twitching in his right eyebrow, and numbness in his foot.

q: What is the name of Lomov's hunting dog?
o: Chisels
Guess
Squeezer
Harness
e: Lomov's beloved hunting dog is named Guess, whom he praises above Chubukov's dog Squeezer.

q: What is the name of Chubukov's hunting dog?
o: Squeezer
Guess
Pug
Mironov
e: Natalya and Chubukov own a young hunting dog named Squeezer.

q: How much money did Lomov pay for Guess?
o: 200 roubles
300 roubles
85 roubles
125 roubles
e: Lomov proudly tells Natalya that he gave 125 roubles for his dog Guess.

q: From whom did Lomov buy his dog Guess?
o: Harness
Count's whipper-in
Mironov
Chubukov
e: Lomov says, "It was a first-rate dog! Why, I gave Mironov 125 roubles for him."

q: How much did Chubukov pay for Squeezer?
o: 45 roubles
125 roubles
85 roubles
185 roubles
e: Natalya says her father gave 85 roubles for Squeezer, claiming Squeezer is "heaps better" than Guess.

q: What physical defect does Lomov say Squeezer has?
o: He has lost his tail
He is overshot (lower jaw shorter than upper)
He is deaf
He is blind in one eye
e: Lomov argues that Squeezer is overshot—his lower jaw is shorter than the upper—so he cannot seize prey properly.

q: Why can Lomov not start shooting right away, even though he wants to go after harvest?
o: His best dog Guess has gone lame
It is snowing heavily
His gun is broken
Chubukov forbade him
e: Lomov explains that his best dog, Guess, has gone lame—either his leg got twisted or another dog bit him.

q: How does Chubukov manage to seal the engagement between Lomov and Natalya at the end?
o: By gifting Oxen Meadows to Lomov
By calling a priest immediately
By selling Squeezer to Lomov
By forcing Natalya's hand into Lomov's as he recovers from fainting
e: As Lomov groggily wakes up, Chubukov thrusts Natalya's hand into his, declares she is willing, and tells them to kiss.

q: What phrase does Chubukov use to describe Natalya's eagerness to marry Lomov?
o: "A silent dove"
"A wise owl"
"A proud queen"
"A lovesick cat"
e: Reassuring Lomov, Chubukov cries, "She's in love; egad, she's like a lovesick cat!"

q: What do Lomov and Natalya argue about in the closing lines even after getting engaged?
o: How much dowry Chubukov will give
Where to hold the wedding
Whether Guess is better or worse than Squeezer
Who will cook the peas
e: Moments after kissing, Natalya insists Guess is worse than Squeezer and Lomov shouts "Better!" as the curtain falls.

q: In Russian naming customs explained in the textbook, what does the patronymic ending "-vitch" (as in Vassilevitch) mean?
o: Brother of
Son of
Friend of
Master of
e: A Russian patronymic ends in "-vitch" for a man, meaning "son of" (e.g., Ivan Vassilevitch = Ivan, son of Vassily).

q: In Russian naming conventions, what does the ending "-ovna" in "Natalya Stepanovna" signify?
o: Daughter of
Mother of
Sister of
Wife of
e: The feminine patronymic suffix "-ovna" means "daughter of" (Natalya Stepanovna = Natalya, daughter of Stepan).

q: Why does Lomov say he must marry because he has reached a "critical age"?
o: He needs to lead a quiet and regular life due to his illnesses
His father left a will forcing him to marry at thirty-five
He wants to travel round Europe
He wants someone to manage his factory in Moscow
e: Lomov believes at thirty-five he ought to lead a quiet, regular life because he suffers from palpitations and nervous sleeplessness.

q: Which three qualities of Natalya does Lomov cite to convince himself she will make an acceptable wife?
o: Wealthy, musical, and soft-spoken
Tall, athletic, and poetic
Submissive, quiet, and fond of dogs
An excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking, and well-educated
e: Lomov tells himself: "She's an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking, well-educated. What more do I want?"

q: What happens to Lomov every night when he tries to sleep, according to his monologue?
o: He walks around the garden for hours
He coughs until sunrise
Something pulls in his side and head, and he jumps up like a lunatic
He sees nightmares about Oxen Meadows
e: Lomov complains that as soon as he starts falling asleep, something gives a pull in his side and shoulder/head, making him jump up like a lunatic.

q: Before the land dispute begins, what farming worry does Natalya share with Lomov?
o: Locusts ate their pea crop
They cut all their hay and fear it may rot in the damp weather
Their wheat was destroyed by frost
Their peasants ran away to the city
e: Natalya mentions they were greedy and had all their hay cut, and now she feels sorry because the weather makes them fear it may rot.

q: What legal threat does Lomov make during the Oxen Meadows argument?
o: To call the Tsar's army
To prove his ownership in court
To burn down the birchwoods
To stop speaking to Chubukov forever
e: Infuriated by Natalya's refusal, Lomov threatens, "I'll prove to you in court that they're mine!"

q: What family scandal does Chubukov hurl at Lomov regarding his younger aunt, Nastasya Mihailovna?
o: She ran away with an architect
She stole Chubukov's horses
She never learnt to read
She went bankrupt in St Petersburg
e: During the insult match, Chubukov taunts Lomov that his younger aunt Nastasya Mihailovna ran away with an architect.

q: What vices does Chubukov accuse Lomov's grandfather and father of having?
o: Bribery and forgery
Smuggling and theft
Cowardice and laziness
His grandfather drank like a fish and his father was a gambler
e: Chubukov shouts that Lomov's whole family were lunatics—his grandfather drank like a fish and his father was a gambler.

q: How does Lomov retaliate with insults against Chubukov's family?
o: Claims Chubukov's brother is in prison
Accuses Natalya of poisoning his cows
Says Chubukov's late wife used to beat him and his grandfather was an embezzler
Calls Chubukov's estate a deserted swamp
e: Lomov retorts that Chubukov's late wife used to beat him and insults Chubukov's relatives as embezzlers and grabbers.

q: Which word used by Chubukov as an insult means a petty, dishonest, quibbling lawyer or schemer?
o: Peasant
Architect
Pettifogger
Hypochondriac
e: Chubukov yells "Pettifogger!" at Lomov—a term for a petty, unscrupulous lawyer who argues over trivial matters.

q: How does Natalya react immediately after Chubukov lets slip that Lomov had come to propose to her?
o: She starts writing him an angry letter
She collapses into an armchair, wails hysterically, and demands her father bring him back
She laughs and refuses to believe it
She locks herself in her bedroom
e: Hearing "To propose!", Natalya falls into an armchair, begins wailing, and cries repeatedly, "Bring him back! Back! Ah! Bring him here!"

q: Whom does Natalya immediately blame when she realises Lomov has left the house?
o: Her father, Chubukov
Herself
Her servant
Lomov's late aunt
e: Despite having argued just as loudly, Natalya accuses her father: "Fetch him! It's your fault! You drove him out!"

q: What melodramatic lament does Chubukov utter when Natalya keeps scolding him to fetch Lomov?
o: "I will move to Moscow tonight!"
"Women should never talk about dogs!"
"I shall sell my estate tomorrow!"
"What a misfortune to be the father of a grown-up daughter! I'll cut my throat!"
e: Overwhelmed by Natalya's hysteria, Chubukov tears his hair and cries, "What a misfortune to be the father of a grown-up daughter! I'll cut my throat!"

q: When Lomov returns, how does Natalya try to change the topic smoothly?
o: She talks about his white gloves
She offers him champagne
She shows him the peas she shelled
She concedes Oxen Meadows are his and asks when he is going shooting
e: Natalya apologizes, yields Oxen Meadows ("Yes, yes, yours!"), and asks politely when he intends to start shooting.

q: According to Natalya, who were Squeezer's purebred parents?
o: Mironov and Guess
Volchanetsky and Rasvachai
Harness and Chisels
Pug and Hound
e: Natalya boasts that Squeezer is a thoroughbred animal, "the son of Harness and Chisels", while Guess's pedigree is unknown.

q: During which famous hunt does Lomov say Guess proved his superiority?
o: The Birchwoods hunt
The Marusinsky hunt
The Burnt Marsh hunt
The Petersburg hunt
e: Lomov boasts that on the Marusinsky hunt, Guess ran neck-and-neck with the Count's dog.

q: How far behind did Squeezer lag on the Marusinsky hunt, according to Lomov?
o: A whole verst behind
Half a mile behind
Ten paces behind
Five dessiatins behind
e: Lomov says while Guess ran neck-and-neck with the Count's dog, "your Squeezer was left a whole verst behind."

q: What embarrassing act does Lomov accuse Squeezer of doing instead of chasing the fox?
o: Running after / worrying a sheep
Falling asleep in the grass
Barking at Chubukov
Stealing bread from the hunter
e: Lomov mocks Squeezer: "He ran after a sheep! ... Yes, while the other dogs ran after the fox!"

q: How does Chubukov excuse the fact that the Count's whipper-in struck Squeezer with his whip?
o: Squeezer was attacking a wolf
The whipper-in was blind
It was an accidental slip in the mud
Everyone is jealous of another person's dog
e: Chubukov defends Squeezer by claiming the Count's whipper-in hit him solely out of envy because everyone is jealous of another's good dog.

q: To what does Lomov unflatteringly compare Squeezer's appearance?
o: A frightened sheep
A newborn mouse
A worn-out cab-horse
A spotted hyena
e: Lomov disparages Squeezer by saying he is "as ugly as a worn-out cab-horse."

q: What breed does Chubukov compare Guess's short muzzle to?
o: A greyhound
A pug
A bulldog
A spaniel
e: Chubukov mocks Guess as old and "as short in the muzzle as a pug."

q: What is a "verst" mentioned in the dog argument?
o: A silver coin smaller than a rouble
A Russian unit of distance, roughly 1.06 km
A type of hunting whistle
A Russian breed of hound
e: A verst is an old Russian unit of distance equal to about 1.06 kilometres (a little over two-thirds of a mile).

q: In the play's glossary, what does "overshot" mean regarding a dog's jaw?
o: Having the upper jaw projecting beyond the lower jaw
Having lost its sense of smell
Having broken teeth
Having an unusually loud bark
e: Lomov explains that Squeezer is "overshot—that is, the lower jaw is shorter than the upper," preventing a strong grip.

q: What dramatic event happens to Lomov at the height of the second argument?
o: He runs out with Guess
He breaks Chubukov's window
He challenges Chubukov to a sword duel
He collapses unconscious into an armchair
e: Exhausted by palpitations, screaming, and numbness, Lomov loses consciousness and collapses in the armchair.

q: How do Chubukov and Natalya react the moment Lomov faints in the chair?
o: They quietly go back to shelling peas
They search his pockets for money
They panic thinking he is dead, scream for water and a doctor
They laugh and lock him in the room
e: Seeing Lomov motionless, Natalya cries "He's dead!" and both frantically call for water and a doctor.

q: What offer does Lomov nervously make about Oxen Meadows before the first quarrel turns vicious?
o: To donate them to the village peasants
To sell them to Natalya for 85 roubles
To make Natalya a present of them on principle
To divide them equally with a fence
e: Lomov insists he does not care about the money and offers, "If you like, I'll make you a present of them," only for Natalya to snap she can gift them herself.

q: What does Chubukov repeatedly ask for to drown out the couple's renewed shouting at the end?
o: Hot tea
Champagne
Cold water
Another lawyer
e: As Natalya and Lomov yell "Worse!" and "Better!", Chubukov tries to shout them down by repeatedly calling for "Champagne! Champagne!"

q: What does Lomov say when Chubukov thrusts Natalya's hand into his right after he regains consciousness?
o: "Eh? What? Who?"
"Bring my dog Guess!"
"Give me three hundred roubles!"
"Where are Oxen Meadows?"
e: Still dazed and seeing "stars and mist," Lomov asks groggily, "Eh? What? Who?" before agreeing and kissing Natalya.

q: How does Lomov first introduce the topic of Oxen Meadows while trying to propose?
o: While comparing hunting trails
While reading his grandfather's will aloud
While accusing Natalya of cutting his hay
While recalling the long friendship and neighbouring land between their two families
e: Trying to lead gracefully to a proposal, Lomov praises their families' close ties and says, "Besides, you know, my Oxen Meadows touch your birchwoods."

q: Read the extract: "And it's impossible for me not to marry. In the first place, I'm already 35... I ought to lead a quiet and regular life." What does this reveal about Lomov's attitude toward marriage?
o: He is deeply swept away by romantic passion
He wants to marry only to acquire Chubukov's birchwoods
He wishes to escape Russia forever
He treats marriage as a practical, health-driven social necessity rather than love
e: Lomov's calculations about age, housekeeping, and sleep show a pragmatic, unromantic view of marriage focused on personal comfort.

q: Read the extract: "My darling! I've been hoping for it for a long time... I've always loved you, my angel, as if you were my own son!" Why is Chubukov's sudden warmth humorous?
o: Because he mistakenly thinks Lomov is Mironov
Because he wants Lomov to marry his aunt instead
Because moments earlier in an aside he suspected Lomov came to borrow money and vowed not to give any
Because Chubukov actually dislikes children
e: Chubukov's aside exposed his suspicion and stinginess; hearing of a marriage proposal flips him instantly into exaggerated affection.

q: When Lomov offers to make Natalya a present of Oxen Meadows, she snaps: "I can make you a present of them myself, because they're mine!" What trait drives both characters here?
o: Deep indifference to land
Stubborn pride and ego over asserting ownership
Selfless generosity
Legal expertise
e: Neither actually refuses the land out of generosity; both insist on being the owner first so they can look superior in granting a favour.

q: In the context of the play, what does "perpetuity" mean in the line "gave the free use of them in perpetuity"?
o: For ever / for an indefinite, unending time
For one single harvest season
Until the bricks are repaid
Under secret legal conditions
e: "In perpetuity" means forever or for an unlimited period without end.

q: Why does Lomov fail to deliver his marriage proposal during his first conversation with Natalya?
o: His nervous roundabout introduction mentions "my Oxen Meadows," igniting an ego clash
Chubukov sends him away immediately
He forgets Natalya's name
Natalya refuses to sit in the room
e: Instead of proposing directly, Lomov nervously brings up family history and neighbouring boundaries, accidentally triggering the land dispute.

q: What does Natalya's instant reversal on Oxen Meadows ("Yes, yes, yours!") after Lomov returns reveal about her priorities?
o: She fears Chubukov will punish her
She checked old land records while he was gone
She wants to trick him into buying Guess
Securing a husband matters far more to her than winning a small strip of meadow
e: Once she learns Lomov came to propose, her desperation to marry immediately overrides her earlier insistence on "principle."

q: How does Lomov's reaction to confrontation illustrate his character as a "hypochondriac"?
o: He calmly quotes medical textbooks
He prescribes medicine to Natalya
Every minor argument immediately triggers exaggerated panic over his heart, numb foot, and eyebrow
He exercises vigorously whenever angry
e: Lomov obsesses over every physical sensation and translates emotional agitation into dramatic medical crises.

q: What tone does Chubukov adopt when calling Natalya a "lovesick cat" in his conversation with Lomov?
o: Grief-stricken and hopeless
Eager, encouraging, and slightly mocking to push the match forward
Formal and distant
Bitterly furious and rejecting
e: Chubukov uses colloquial exaggeration to reassure a hesitant suitor that Natalya will gladly say yes without delay.

q: In the line "I've never seen such impudence!", what does "impudence" mean in context?
o: Generous hospitality
Shameless rudeness or disrespect
Great wisdom
Quiet shyness
e: "Impudence" refers to insolent, disrespectful boldness—each character sees the other's claims as brazen rudeness.

q: Why does Natalya blame Chubukov ("You drove him out!") even though she argued just as bitterly with Lomov?
o: In sudden distress over losing a suitor, she deflects guilt onto her father
Chubukov had locked the front door before she entered
Chubukov promised Oxen Meadows to Mironov
She never spoke a word during the argument
e: Natalya's volatile emotions make her blind to her own role in driving Lomov away, scapegoating her father instead.

q: Why does Chubukov's dialogue "What a weight off my shoulders, O Lord!" reveal his true attitude toward Natalya's marriage?
o: He hates having neighbours live nearby
He wanted Natalya to become a nun
He cannot afford peas for his kitchen
He views an unmarried adult daughter as a stressful burden he is desperate to hand over
e: Throughout the play, Chubukov sighs over the "misfortune" of having a grown-up daughter, viewing her marriage mainly as his own relief.

q: Why do Lomov and Natalya immediately start arguing about hunting dogs once Oxen Meadows is settled?
o: Because both are secretly planning to open a kennel
Because even casual small talk triggers their competitive pride over anything they own
Because Guess bit Squeezer outside the room
Because Chubukov ordered them to compare dogs
e: Natalya brings up shooting only to keep conversation going, yet Lomov's praise of Guess provokes her competitive pride on behalf of Squeezer.

q: What does Chubukov mean when he calls Lomov a "grabber"?
o: A skilled hunter
A generous guest
A greedy person trying to seize someone else's rightful property
A nervous dancer
e: "Grabber" accuses Lomov of greedily trying to snatch land that Chubukov insists belongs to his own family.

q: Read the extract: "You're a malicious, double-faced intriguer!" What does "malicious" mean here?
o: Fond of music
Physically weak
Full of spite and intent to harm others
Extremely forgetful
e: "Malicious" means driven by malice—wishing or intending to cause harm or distress.

q: What contrast is highlighted when Natalya enters in an apron while Lomov stands in white gloves and an evening jacket?
o: Youthful bravery versus elderly cowardice
Practical everyday domesticity versus stiff, anxious ceremonial formality
Rich city merchant versus poor peasant
Religious devotion versus scientific logic
e: Natalya is caught mid-chore shelling peas, contrasting humorously with Lomov's overly formal attire meant for a grand proposal.

q: Why does Chubukov's exclamation "I'm the most unhappy of men! Why don't I put a bullet into my brain?" produce comic effect rather than tragedy?
o: Because his suicidal exaggeration is a wildly disproportionate reaction to a petty household quarrel
Because the play is set in summer
Because he has no gun in Russia
Because Lomov laughs loudly at him
e: The absurd mismatch between a minor bickering session and dramatic threats of suicide creates pure farce.

q: In the context of Chubukov's words, why does he accuse Lomov of talking "like an old woman"?
o: Because Lomov wears a scarf
Because Lomov praises Natalya's cooking
Because Lomov offers him peas
Because Lomov keeps whining about his failing health, gossiping, and dragging out trivial complaints
e: Chubukov mocks Lomov's petty, complaining bickering and endless health grievances as unmanly nagging.

q: What does Lomov mean when he insists he is "acting on principle" regarding Oxen Meadows?
o: He is reading from a philosophy book
He wants to follow Russian agricultural laws carefully
He intends to donate the Meadows to charity
He refuses to let anyone falsely deny his rightful claim, regardless of the small cash value
e: Both Lomov and Natalya claim "principle" to justify why they fight tooth and nail over land worth barely 300 roubles.

q: Why does the playwright include Chubukov's brief aside ("He's come to borrow money. Shan't give him any!") near the start?
o: To prove Lomov is actually bankrupt
To explain Russian banking rules
To let the audience see Chubukov's cynical suspicion beneath his overly sweet greetings
To introduce a fourth character
e: The aside reveals Chubukov's insincerity right away, making his sudden shift to calling Lomov "angel" doubly comic.

q: Which detail best shows that Lomov does NOT abandon his argumentative nature even while physically collapsing?
o: He silently writes a cheque for 300 roubles
Even while clutching his heart and staggering out, he keeps shouting insults and claiming Guess is better
He bows politely to Natalya
He asks for a blanket before leaving
e: Each time Lomov cries that his heart is bursting, his pride drags him right back into shouting another retort.

q: Why does Natalya ask, "Are you going to a ball or what?" upon seeing Lomov?
o: Formal evening dress and white gloves are absurdly out of place for a casual daytime neighbourly visit
She never saw white gloves before
She wants him to invite her to a party in town
She thinks he is dressed as a waiter
e: Neighbours visiting each other in the countryside normally wore everyday clothes, so Lomov's ceremonial outfit looks unusual.

q: What triggers Chubukov's sudden shift from calling Lomov "my dear fellow" to yelling abuse in the Oxen Meadows quarrel?
o: Lomov speaks rudely to him ("Shut up! Don't shout!") and refuses to yield the Meadows
Lomov refuses to drink tea
Natalya breaks a plate
Guess barks outside the window
e: Chubukov initially expects a polite request, but once Lomov raises his voice and refuses to back down, Chubukov loses all restraint.

q: In "You've simply got the habit of contradicting everything", what irony lies in Natalya's accusation against Lomov?
o: Chubukov never interrupts anyone
Natalya wants to move to Moscow
Lomov always agrees with whatever Natalya says
Natalya herself is equally stubborn and refuses to give an inch in every argument
e: Natalya accuses Lomov of the exact quarrelsome stubbornness that she herself displays throughout the play.

q: Why does Chekhov have Natalya and Lomov argue over Mironov's 125 roubles versus Chubukov's 85 roubles?
o: To prove dogs were expensive in Russia
To teach students how to calculate profit
To show how petty landowners turn even minor purchases into status symbols and ego battles
Because Mironov was Natalya's uncle
e: Natalya calls 125 roubles absurdly overpriced compared to 85 roubles, while Lomov equates higher price with superior breeding.

q: What role does the "Count's whipper-in" anecdote serve in Lomov's argument about Squeezer?
o: To praise Chubukov's horse-riding
To cite an outside authority's action as proof that Squeezer behaved foolishly during a real hunt
To ask Chubukov to hire a whipper-in
To describe how Guess became lame
e: Lomov brings up the Marusinsky hunt incident—where Squeezer chased a sheep and got whipped—as factual proof of Squeezer's inferiority.

q: Why does Chubukov stop attacking Lomov and rush to unite the couple the instant Lomov wakes from his faint?
o: He wants to leave for the market immediately
He fears another argument will ruin the match permanently and leave Natalya unmarried on his hands

Wealthy landowners who treat marriage as an economic convenience while fighting blindly over petty pride and property

o: Men aged thirty-five lost voting rights if unmarried
Only people over fifty could marry in Russia
Thirty-five was the legal retirement age for landowners
Marriage for gentry men was treated as a social and domestic milestone tied to settling down rather than emotional intimacy
e: Lomov treats marriage as a practical deadline for health and household management, reflecting social convention over romance.

q: Why does the dog quarrel appear even more absurd than the Oxen Meadows quarrel?
o: Because neither family actually owned a dog
Because dogs are forbidden inside drawing rooms
Because Guess is already old and lame and Squeezer cost just 85 roubles, so zero economic stake justifies their fury
Because Mironov already solved the dog argument
e: Land at least carries long-term estate boundaries; risking a marriage over a lame dog and an 85-rouble pup highlights pure vanity.

q: Which quality is shared equally by all three characters—Lomov, Natalya, and Chubukov—despite their mutual hostility?
o: Deep scholarly humility
Unconditional affection for neighbours
Quick-tempered pride combined with shameless readiness to reverse stance for self-interest
Calm self-restraint under stress
e: All three flare up instantly over petty ego yet abandon pride whenever marriage or gain demands it.

q: How does Chekhov use rapid dialogue interruptions and mirroring to heighten comic tension?
o: It makes every line sound like formal legal poetry
Characters cut each other off mid-thought and echo words ("Better!" / "Worse!"), creating breathless rhythmic chaos
It slows down the scene so audiences can take notes
It turns the play into a silent pantomime
e: Overlapping retorts, mimicking, and rapid repetition mirror childish squabbling and keep the farce moving at breakneck pace.

q: What does Chubukov's aside ("He's come to borrow money. Shan't give him any!") reveal beneath the hospitable greetings of Russian gentry?
o: Suspicion, stinginess, and mercenary calculation masked by exaggerated terms of affection
Complete trust and shared finances among neighbours
Total ignorance of money
Fear of foreign invaders
e: The contrast between "my darling" spoken aloud and "shan't give him any" thought silently exposes hollow social politeness.

q: In what crucial way does Lomov's fainting fit serve as the turning point (catalyst) of the plot?
o: It convinces Natalya to become a doctor
It forces Mironov to return 125 roubles
It ends the play sadly with Lomov's funeral
The sudden shock of thinking he is dead silences the dog quarrel and lets Chubukov rush the engagement before arguing resumes
e: Because words fail to resolve any dispute, only Lomov's physical collapse interrupts the fight long enough for Chubukov to join their hands.

q: How would you critically evaluate Chubukov's role as a parent in "The Proposal"?
o: Strict moral philosopher who forbids materialism
Wise, impartial mediator who teaches patience
Absent and completely unaware of Natalya's wishes
Volatile and self-serving: he inflames his daughter's petty quarrel, then panics and pushes her into a turbulent match to relieve his burden
e: Chubukov worsens the conflict by joining the insults, then prioritizes unloading his "burden" over his daughter's long-term happiness.

q: Why does Chekhov make Natalya call herself "willing" right after demanding Lomov return, even though she still despises Guess?
o: She has secretly fallen in love with Guess
Lomov gave her five dessiatins of wheat
Societal pressure on an unmarried twenty-five-year-old woman outweighs personal harmony or affection
She plans to leave Chubukov's estate permanently
e: Fear of remaining unmarried at twenty-five drives Natalya to secure the proposal regardless of blatant incompatibility.

q: Which detail shows that anger temporarily overrides Lomov's obsession with his weak health?
o: He refuses to drink water when offered
Even after shouting that his heart is bursting and his foot is asleep, he keeps turning back to hurl one more insult
He carries Chubukov out of the room
He runs two versts in snow
e: His wounded ego keeps pulling him back into the verbal brawl despite his dramatic complaints of imminent collapse.

q: Which proverb best encapsulates the final scene of "The Proposal" where the couple resumes fighting over Guess and Squeezer?
o: Old habits die hard (quarrelsome natures do not vanish with an engagement)
Fortune favours the brave
A stitch in time saves nine
All that glitters is not gold
e: An engagement kiss cannot cure deep-seated stubbornness; both characters instantly revert to bickering over their dogs.

q: How does the mention of "champagne" at the end echo the earlier farce of Lomov's "evening dress"?
o: Both are symbols of Russian military victory
Both represent hollow aristocratic ceremony trying to disguise vulgar, chaotic reality
Both show Lomov is a French citizen
Both belong to Chubukov's hunting club
e: Just as formal evening attire masks a childish brawl, celebratory champagne masks a loveless, shouting engagement.

q: Why does Chekhov avoid introducing any sensible outsider (like a priest, judge, or neutral friend) to mediate the quarrel?
o: To keep the cast small and focus relentlessly on how the trio generate and resolve their own absurdity
Because priests were absent from Russian villages
Because a judge arrives in Act Two
Because the play was written for only one actor
e: Restricting the action to three equally flawed characters creates a self-contained comedy of mutual folly.

q: What insight about communication breakdown is highlighted by the transition from "My Oxen Meadows touch your birchwoods" to "My foot's gone to sleep"?
o: Short speeches always fail in drama
Landowners should never discuss farming outdoors
Physical exercise prevents misunderstandings
Indirect hints mixed with possessiveness ("my") derail sensitive goals when pride replaces active listening
e: A single possessive pronoun ("my") triggers defensive pride, derailing the entire conversation away from marriage.

q: If Natalya had politely ignored the phrase "my Oxen Meadows" during Lomov's first visit, what most likely would have happened?
o: Chubukov would have lent Lomov 300 roubles
Lomov would have immediately left without saying anything
Lomov would have stated his proposal far earlier without getting thrown out, though future quarrels would still loom
Guess and Squeezer would never be mentioned anywhere
e: Avoiding the initial land clash would have allowed Lomov to finish his proposal speech, though their temperament suggests conflict would still surface later.

q: What makes Chubukov's final words—"Champagne! Champagne!"—function as comic punctuation rather than genuine celebration?
o: Lomov is allergic to champagne
He shouts it desperately over the couple's continued screaming about Guess and Squeezer, exposing his relief as premature
Natalya asks for pea soup instead
He does not actually own any champagne in his cellar
e: Shouting "Champagne!" as an attempted fanfare while his future son-in-law and daughter keep brawling underlines the play's satirical punchline.

q: In CBSE/JAC competency perspective, which single lesson best applies Chekhov's satire in "The Proposal" to everyday life?
o: Formal evening clothes should never be worn before sunset
Letting ego and stubbornness over trivial matters dominate relationships destroys peace and dignity
Always check property papers before visiting neighbours
Never buy hunting dogs worth more than eighty-five roubles
e: Chekhov demonstrates with comic exaggeration how petty ego and unwillingness to compromise poison human relationships.
